label: thm:counterexample
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:counterexample}
There exist abrupt symmetric pure-jump L\'evy processes for which $\mathfrak{s}_1(0)=\infty$, $\mathfrak{s}_1(r)<\infty$ for $r\in\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0\}$ and $\mathfrak{s}_1\in L^1_\mathrm{loc}(\mathbb{R})$.
head: environment
name: Vigon's conjecture fails

label: thm:cantor-exceptional-slopes
title: Theorem
head: environment

label: rem:counterexample
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:counterexample}
\textbf{(a)} Theorems~\ref{thm:counterexample} and
\ref{thm:cantor-exceptional-slopes} show two different levels of failure of Vigon's conjecture. Theorem~\ref{thm:counterexample} gives the particularly simple symmetric situation in which the exceptional set is the singleton $\{0\}$, whereas Theorem~\ref{thm:cantor-exceptional-slopes} shows that the exceptional set may instead be uncountable and perfect. Thus, pointwise finiteness of $\mathfrak{s}_1$ can depend on the drift in a substantially more complicated way than local integrability alone suggests.\\
\textbf{(b)} The constructions are not canonical. Their proofs use quantitative separation between successive jump scales, together with corresponding balance conditions on the masses and, in the asymmetric construction, on the drift parameters. These conditions leave considerable freedom in the choice of the defining sequences. Thus, the particular parameters used in Theorems~\ref{thm:counterexample} and~\ref{thm:cantor-exceptional-slopes} are chosen for convenience rather than being intrinsic to the phenomenon. \\
\textbf{(c)} The counterexamples may also be chosen with L\'evy measures having $C^\infty$ densities on $\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0\}$. This can be achieved by replacing the atoms by suitably chosen smooth bumps, in the spirit of the construction in Section~\ref{subsec:full-index-region}. In the interest of brevity, the details are omitted in the present work.\\
\textbf{(d)} Theorem~\ref{thm:counterexample} has a particularly striking interpretation in terms of point hitting and local times. Since $\mathfrak{s}_1(r)<\infty$ if and only if $X^{(r)}=(X_t-rt)_{t\geqslant0}$ hits points, the process $X$ itself does not hit points and has no local time field, whereas every non-zero linear drift perturbation $X^{(r)}$ hits points and admits a local time field; see the discussion following~\cite[Conj.~1.10]{MR4828847} and the references therein.

More generally, for the process in Theorem~\ref{thm:cantor-exceptional-slopes}, the drift perturbation $X^{(r)}$ fails to hit points precisely for $r\in E$, while it hits points for every $r\notin E$. Hence the existence of a local time field may vary over an uncountable set of deterministic slopes.

This has a natural interpretation in terms of local times along curves: the local time of $X^{(r)}$ at level $a$ is the local time of $X$ along the affine line $t\mapsto a+rt$. Thus, even within the class of straight lines, existence of local times may depend delicately on the slope. This connects the examples with the study of local times along curves. Bass and Burdzy~\cite{MR4901629} establish continuity and uniform boundedness of Brownian local times over bounded H\"older classes with exponent greater than $1/2$, while Holden and Sheffield~\cite{MR4055190} obtain analogous occupation-density estimates for certain Gaussian fields under Lipschitz perturbations. Our examples show that for infinite-variation L\'evy processes even the existence of a local time field need not be stable under deterministic linear perturbations.

label: cor:hulls
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:hulls}
Let $X$ be a real L\'evy process of infinite variation. Exactly one of the following holds:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}, leftmargin=2em]
\item $X$ is abrupt, $\mathrm{d} C_T'$ is purely atomic and its atoms are isolated in $(0,T)$ a.s.
\item $X$ is strongly eroded, $\mathrm{d} C_T'$ is diffuse, singular continuous and $C_T$ is continuously differentiable a.s.
\end{enumerate}
Moreover, the dichotomy is independent of $T\in(0,\infty)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By Theorem~\ref{thm:dichotomy}, it suffices to show that abrupt L\'evy processes satisfy (i) and strongly eroded processes satisfy (ii). The convex function $C_T$ admits a right-continuous right-derivative $C_T'$ on $(0,T)$. Denote its range (image) by $S_T\subset \mathbb{R}$ and let $\mathcal{L}(S_T)\subset\mathbb{R}$ denote its set of finite limit points. According to~\cite[Thms~1.1 and~1.2]{MR4828847}, abrupt L\'evy processes satisfy $\mathcal{L}(S_T)=\emptyset$ and $\mathrm{d} C_T'$ puts positive mass at all jump times of $C_T'$. If there existed some accumulation $t\in(0,T)$ of jump times $t_n$ of $C_T'$, since $C_T'$ is locally bounded, then $C_T'(t_n)$ would have a convergent subsequence, contradicting $\mathcal{L}(S_T)=\emptyset$. Thus, $\mathrm{d} C_T'$ is purely atomic, and its atoms are isolated. (Note that the atoms do accumulate at $0$ and $T$.) 

Again by~\cite[Thms~1.1 and~1.2]{MR4828847}, for a strongly eroded L\'evy processes, $\mathcal{L}(S_T)=\mathbb{R}$ and $C'_T$ is continuous. Thus, $\mathrm{d} C'_T$ is diffuse. Moreover, the stick-breaking representation in~\cite[Thm~3.1]{MR4448688} shows that the sum of the lengths of maximal intervals of constancy of $C'_T$ (where $C_T'$ is differentiable with $C_T''=0$) equals $T$, making $\mathrm{d} C'_T$ a singular continuous measure.
head: environment

label: rem:hulls
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:hulls}
\textbf{(a)} By~\cite[Cor.~1.13 and~1.14]{MR4828847}, a dichotomy completely analogous to the one in Corollary~\ref{cor:hulls} holds over infinite time horizons.\\
\textbf{(b)} By~\cite[Prop.~1.5]{MR4828847}, if two L\'evy processes differ by a finite-variation process, then both processes fall in the same category in both Theorem~\ref{thm:dichotomy} and Corollary~\ref{cor:hulls}.\\
\textbf{(c)} A minor modification of the arguments in the proof of Corollary~\ref{cor:hulls} shows that the statement in~\cite[Conj.~1.9]{MR4828847} is equivalent to the dichotomy that the convex minorant $C_T$ of any infinite-variation L\'evy process is either continuously differentiable a.s. or $\mathrm{d} C_T'$ is purely atomic with isolated atoms a.s. In fact, this is further equivalent to the dichotomy (see also~\cite[Tab.~1]{MR4828847}): for infinite-variation L\'evy processes, the finite limit set $\mathcal{L}(S_T)$ of the slopes of the convex minorant $C_T$ is either $\emptyset$ a.s. or $\mathbb{R}$ a.s.

label: thm:all-beta
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:all-beta}
Let $X$ be a L\'evy process of infinite variation. If $X$ is strongly eroded, then $\beta_-\in[0,1]$ and $\beta_+\in[1,2]$. Conversely, for every pair $(b_-, b_+)\in[0,1]\times[1,2]$, there exists a symmetric strongly eroded process with $\beta_-=b_-$ and $\beta_+=b_+$. Moreover, its L\'evy measure can be chosen to have a strictly positive $C^\infty$ density on $\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0\}$, in which case the process has bounded $C^\infty$ transition densities with bounded derivatives of every order at all positive times.

body_md:
\label{app:cor:lipschitz}
Suppose that $X$ has infinite variation, then exactly one of the following holds.
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=2em, label=\textup{(\alph*)}]
\item The process $X$ is abrupt, $\mathcal Z_\ell$ is locally finite almost surely for each $\ell>|m|$ and
\[
 \bigcup_{\ell>|m|}\mathcal Z_\ell
 =\{t\in\mathbb{R} : t\text{ is a local infimum of }X\}\quad\text{is countable almost surely}.
\] 
\item The process $X$ is strongly eroded and $\mathcal Z_\ell$ has zero Lebesgue measure but is not locally finite almost surely for each $\ell>|m|$. 
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
If $X$ is abrupt,~\cite[Thm~5.5]{MR3176366} places each contact point $t$ among its local infima. Every contact point is isolated by~\cite[Thm~3.1]{MR3176366}, making $\mathcal Z_\ell$ locally finite. The union identity follows from~\cite[Thm~5.5]{MR3176366}.

Since $\mathcal Z_\ell$ is closed and regenerative by~\cite[Thm~2.6]{MR3176366}, then the set is equal to the range of a subordinator (see, e.g.~\cite{MR350879, MR256460}). For a strongly eroded process,~\cite[Thm~4.7]{MR3176366} shows that the associated subordinator is not compound Poisson, making $\mathcal Z_\ell$ a perfect set. This set has zero Lebesgue measure by~\cite[Thms~4.1]{MR3176366} because $X$ is of infinite variation.

label: app:cor:burgers
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{app:cor:burgers}
Let $X$ have infinite variation and satisfy~\eqref{app:eq:subquadratic}. For every fixed $t>0$, exactly one of the following alternatives holds almost surely.
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin =2em, label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item $X$ is abrupt, the set $\mathcal A_t$ is locally finite and $\mathcal A_{0,t}$ is regenerative.
\item $X$ is strongly eroded, there are no rarefaction intervals and $a_t$ is strictly increasing on $\mathbb{R}$.
\end{enumerate}
In particular, the abrupt case admits rarefaction intervals, whereas the strongly eroded case does not.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Theorem~\ref{thm:dichotomy} gives the two possible classes of $X$. In the abrupt class, apply~\cite[Thms~4.3 and~4.6]{MR3082645}. In the strongly eroded class, $X$ is eroded, so~\cite[Thm~4.8]{MR3082645} excludes rarefaction intervals. The map $a_t$ is nondecreasing, so the absence of constant intervals is equivalent to strict increase. (The results of~\cite{MR3082645} stated at time one apply at time $t$ by replacing the potential with $tX$, which satisfies~\eqref{app:eq:subquadratic} and is in the same class as $X$.) Finally, in the abrupt case, $a_t(x)\in\mathcal A_t$ and the map is right-continuous. Since $\mathcal A_t$ is locally finite, for each $x$ there is $\varepsilon>0$ such that $a_t(z)=a_t(x)$ for $x\leqslant z<x+\varepsilon$. Hence rarefaction intervals occur. This also shows directly that the two geometric alternatives are mutually exclusive.

label: lem:smoothed
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $\int_{(-1,1)}x^2 \nu(\mathrm{d} x)<\infty$, differentiation under the integrals in~\eqref{eq:HD} is justified on compact subintervals of $(0,\infty)$. First, note that $f:u\mapsto\sigma^2 u$ satisfies $f'(u)=u^{-1}f(u)$. Second, 
\[
f:(x,u)\mapsto \frac{ux^2}{1+u^2x^2}
\quad\text{satisfies}\quad
\bigg|\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d} u}f(x,u)\bigg| = \bigg|\frac{x^2 (1-u^2x^2)}{(1+u^2x^2)^2}\bigg|
\leqslant u^{-1}f(u,x).
\]
Altogether, $|H'(u)| \leqslant u^{-1}H(u)$ for $u>0$, concluding the first part of~\eqref{eq:HD-derivative}. Next, since $2|ux|\leqslant1+u^2x^2$, then $2u^2|x|^3/(1+u^2x^2)^2 \leqslant ux^2/(1+u^2x^2)$ and hence $|uD'(u)|\leqslant H(u)$ for $u>0$, proving~\eqref{eq:HD-derivative}.

Using~\eqref{eq:HD-derivative}, we find that
\[
\left|\log \frac{H(v)}{H(u)}\right|
=
\left|\int_u^v \frac{H'(t)}{H(t)}\,\mathrm{d} t\right|
\leqslant
\int_u^v\frac{\mathrm{d} t}{t}
=
\log(v/u)
\leqslant\log2,
\] 
which gives the first half of~\eqref{eq:dyadic-HD}. Similarly,~\eqref{eq:HD-derivative} gives $|D'(t)|\leqslant H(t)/t$ and, since $H(t)\leqslant2H(u)$ for every $t\in[u,v]\subset[u,2u]$, the second half of~\eqref{eq:HD-derivative} follows:
\[
|D(v)-D(u)|
\leqslant\int_u^v |D'(t)| \mathrm{d} t \leqslant
\int_u^v\frac{H(t)}{t}\mathrm{d} t \leqslant
2H(u)\int_u^v\frac{\mathrm{d} t}{t} =
2H(u)\log(v/u) \leqslant
2(\log2)H(u).
\]

By definition of $D$, it follows directly, that 
\begin{equation*}
\psi(uz)-iuzD(u)= -\frac{1}{2}\sigma^2u^2z^2+ \int_{(-1,1)} \left(e^{iuzx}-1-\frac{iuzx}{1+u^2x^2}\right) \nu(\mathrm{d} x).
\end{equation*} 
Hence, since the Gaussian remainder is numerically at most $\sigma^2u^2/2$, it remains to bound the integrand inside the integral in the expression above. For $|z|\leqslant1$ and $y\in\mathbb{R}$, it follows that
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:elementary-Taylor}
\left|e^{izy}-1-\frac{izy}{1+y^2}\right|
\leqslant5\frac{y^2}{1+y^2}.
\end{equation}
Indeed, for $|y|\leqslant1$, subtracting and adding $izy$, and applying the triangle inequality, implies that
\begin{equation*}
\left|e^{izy}-1-\frac{izy}{1+y^2}\right| 
\leqslant |e^{izy}-1-izy|+|zy|\left|1-\frac{1}{1+y^2}\right| 
\leqslant \frac{y^2}{2}+\frac{|y|^3}{1+y^2}
\leqslant \frac{3y^2}{2}.
\end{equation*}
For $|y|>1$, the triangle inequality implies directly, that $|e^{izy}-1-izy/(1+y^2)| \leqslant 2+|y|/(1+y^2)\leqslant 5/2$, and since $y^2/(1+y^2) \geqslant 1/2$ for all $|y|>1$, we can conclude~\eqref{eq:elementary-Taylor}. Substituting $y=ux$ in~\eqref{eq:compact-exponent} and applying~\eqref{eq:elementary-Taylor}, proves~\eqref{eq:smoothed-approximation}.

Put $\operatorname{sinc} y=\sin(y)/y$ for $y\ne0$, with $\operatorname{sinc}0=1$. Note, that
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:sinc-bound}
1-|\operatorname{sinc} y|\geqslant\frac18\frac{y^2}{1+y^2}, \quad \text{for all }y \in \mathbb{R}.
\end{equation}
Indeed, if $|y|\leqslant2$, then $\operatorname{sinc} y\geqslant0$ and $1-|\operatorname{sinc} y|=1-\operatorname{sinc} y$. Hence, the alternating Taylor bound gives $1-\operatorname{sinc} y
\geqslant y^2/6- y^4/120
\geqslant 2y^2/15
\geqslant (1/8)y^2/(1+y^2)$. If $|y|\geqslant2$, then $|\operatorname{sinc} y|
=|\sin y|/|y|
\leqslant |y|^{-1}
\leqslant1/2$, and therefore $1-|\operatorname{sinc} y|
\geqslant 1/2
\geqslant(1/8)y^2/(1+y^2)$. Hence,~\eqref{eq:sinc-bound} implies for all $y \in \mathbb{R}$, that
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:ineq_cos_sinc}
\begin{aligned}
\int_{-1}^1(1-\cos(zy))\mathrm{d} z
&=2(1-\operatorname{sinc} y)
\geqslant\frac14\frac{y^2}{1+y^2},\quad \text{and}\\
\int_1^2(1-\cos(zy))\mathrm{d} z
&=1-\cos(3y/2)\operatorname{sinc}(y/2)
\geqslant\frac1{32}\frac{y^2}{1+y^2}.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
Since $Q(u)=\sigma^2u^2/2+\int_{(-1,1)} (1-\cos(ux))\nu(\mathrm{d} x)$, Tonelli's theorem, together with~\eqref{eq:ineq_cos_sinc} proves~\eqref{eq:smoothed-average} for the jump part, where the Gaussian average can be calculated directly to be $\sigma^2u^2/3$ and $7\sigma^2u^2/6$, so the same constant $c_0$ works for both parts, concluding both estimates in~\eqref{eq:smoothed-average}.

For the lower bound in~\eqref{eq:P-comparison}, the first average in~\eqref{eq:smoothed-average} gives  $c_0uH(u)
\leqslant \int_{-1}^1Q(zu)\mathrm{d} z
\leqslant 2P(u)$, while~\eqref{eq:smoothed-approximation} at $z=1$ gives $u|D(u)|\leqslant P(u)+C_0uH(u)$. Thus,
\[
u(|D(u)|+H(u))
=u|D(u)|-C_0uH(u)
+(1+C_0)uH(u)
\leqslant P(u) + 2\frac{1+C_0}{c_0}P(u)
=\frac{2+2C_0+c_0}{c_0}P(u),
\]
implying the lower bound in~\eqref{eq:P-comparison}. The upper bound in~\eqref{eq:P-comparison} follows by taking the supremum in~\eqref{eq:smoothed-approximation}.

If $\sigma=0$, another application of Tonelli gives
\[
 \int_1^\infty H(u)\frac{\mathrm{d} u}{u}
 =\int_{(-1,1)}|x|
       \left(\frac\pi2-\arctan|x|\right)\nu(\mathrm{d} x),
\] where we know that $(\pi/2-\arctan|x|) \in [\pi/4,\pi/2]$ for all $|x|<1$. If $\sigma>0$, the Gaussian contribution to the integral is infinite. The usual finite-variation criterion, i.e. that the process has finite variation if and only if $\sigma=0$ and $\int_{(-1,1)}|x|\nu(\mathrm{d} x)<\infty$, therefore proves~\eqref{eq:variation-H}; see~\cite{MR1406564,Sato1999}.

label: lem:energy-escape
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For $s\geqslant0$, define locally within this proof $R(s)=(H(e^s)^2+D(e^s)^2)^{1/2}$. Since \(H,D\in C^1((0,\infty))\) and \(H(e^s)>0\), the vector \((H(e^s),D(e^s))\) never vanishes. Hence, since  \(R(s)=\sqrt{H(e^s)^2+D(e^s)^2}\) is continuously differentiable on \([0,\infty)\). Inequality~\eqref{eq:HD-derivative}, implies that, for all $s \geqslant 0$, 
\[
|R'(s)|=
\left|\frac{
H(e^s)\,e^sH'(e^s)
+
D(e^s)\,e^sD'(e^s)
}{
\sqrt{H(e^s)^2+D(e^s)^2}}\right|
\leqslant\sqrt2\,H(e^s),\quad \text{and}\quad 
\left|\frac{\mathrm{d} }{\mathrm{d} s}\arctan R(s)\right|
\leqslant\frac{\sqrt2 H(e^s)}{1+R(s)^2}.
\]
Condition~\eqref{eq:finite-energy} makes $\varpi:s \mapsto \arctan R(s)$ be of finite total variation on $[0,\infty)$ since $\int_0^\infty |\varpi'(s)| \mathrm{d} s<\infty$. In particular, $|\varpi(t)-\varpi(s)| \leqslant \int_s^t |\varpi'(r)| \mathrm{d} r$ for \(t>s\), and the right-hand side tends to \(0\) as \(s\to\infty\), uniformly in \(t\geqslant s\). Thus, $\varpi$ admits a limit in $[0,\pi/2]$ at infinity. A limit strictly less than $\pi/2$ would make $R$ eventually bounded, and therefore~\eqref{eq:finite-energy} would imply $\int_0^\infty H(e^s)\mathrm{d} s<\infty$, contradicting~\eqref{eq:variation-H}. Thus, $R(s)\to\infty$. The first conclusion $H(u)+|D(u)| \to \infty$ as $u \to \infty$ follows directly, where $P(u)/u\to \infty$ as $u \to \infty$ follows from~\eqref{eq:P-comparison}, concluding the proof.

label: lem:increment
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Using the L\'evy--Khintchine representation, the drift terms cancel and
\begin{equation*}
    \psi(u+v)-\psi(u)-\psi(v) =
-\sigma^2uv
+
\int_{(-1,1)}
(e^{iux}-1)(e^{ivx}-1)\nu(\mathrm{d} x).
\end{equation*}
Hence, by the triangle inequality and applying Cauchy--Schwarz twice, it follows for all $u,v \in \mathbb{R}$, that
\begin{align*}
\left|\psi(u+v)-\psi(u)-\psi(v)\right|
&\leqslant
\sigma^2|uv|
+
\bigg(\int_{(-1,1)}|e^{iux}-1|^2\nu(\mathrm{d} x)\bigg)^{1/2}
\bigg(\int_{(-1,1)}|e^{ivx}-1|^2\nu(\mathrm{d} x)\bigg)^{1/2}\\
&\leqslant
\bigg(
\sigma^2u^2+
\int_{(-1,1)}|e^{iux}-1|^2\nu(\mathrm{d} x)
\bigg)^{1/2}
\bigg(
\sigma^2v^2+
\int_{(-1,1)}|e^{ivx}-1|^2\nu(\mathrm{d} x)
\bigg)^{1/2}.
\end{align*}
Since $|e^{iy}-1|^2=2(1-\cos y)$, and $Q(u) =-\Re\psi(u) =\sigma^2u^2/2 +\int_{(-1,1)}(1-\cos(ux))\nu(\mathrm{d} x)$, we have $\sigma^2u^2 +\int_{(-1,1)}|e^{iux}-1|^2\nu(\mathrm{d} x) =2Q(u)$ and similarly for $v$. Thus,~\eqref{eq:increment} follows.

Since $\Re\psi(w)=-Q(w)$,~\eqref{eq:increment} gives $|Q(u+v)-Q(u)-Q(v)| \leqslant 2\sqrt{Q(u)Q(v)}$. Thus, 
\[
                                       
Q(u)+Q(v)-2\sqrt{Q(u)Q(v)}
\leqslant
Q(u+v)
\leqslant
Q(u)+Q(v)+2\sqrt{Q(u)Q(v)}.                                         
\qedhere
\]

label: lem:local-average
title: Lemma
head: environment

label: eq:delta-epsilon
title: Proof
body_md:
Write $I=(a,b)$, $L=b-a$, $R=\max\{1,|a|,|b|\}$ and $K=4(M+R+1)$. Fix
\begin{equation}\label{eq:delta-epsilon}
 \delta=\min\left\{1,\frac{K}{4C_0},\frac{L}{256C_0}\right\},
 \quad \text{and}\quad 
 \varepsilon=\min\left\{1,\frac{c_0\delta}{16},
                            \frac{L}{256}\right\}.
\end{equation}
All constants below are independent of the frequency $u$. We split the proof of~\eqref{eq:local-average} into two parts, according to the size of $Q(u)/u$.

\textbf{Part 1.} Suppose $Q(u)/u\geqslant\varepsilon$. For $u\geqslant1$, it follows by assumptions that $a(u)=(1+Q(u))/u\in[\varepsilon,M+1]$ and $|b(u)|=|B(u)|/u\leqslant M$, so
\[
 \Phi_I(u)\geqslant
 \frac{L\varepsilon}{(M+1)^2+(R+M)^2}\eqqcolon c_1>0.
\] The constant $c_1$ depends only on $I$, $M$ and $\varepsilon$, and in particular is independent of $u$. Since $w\mapsto\Phi_I(w)$ is continuous on $(0,\infty)$, for each such $u$ there exists $\eta_u>0$ such that $\Phi_I(w)\geqslant c_1/2$ whenever $|w-u|<2\eta_u$. Set  $r=\min\{\eta_u/u,1/10\}>0$ note that $\Phi_I(w)\geqslant c_1/2$ for $w\in J_u\coloneqq ((1-r)u,(1+r)u)$, and hence $\int_{J_u}\Phi_I(w)\,\mathrm{d} w\geqslant c_1ru$. Thus,~\eqref{eq:local-average} holds in the regime $Q(u)/u\geqslant\varepsilon$, with a constant independent of $u$.

\textbf{Part 2.}
It remains to consider the case $Q(u)/u<\varepsilon$.
Set
\[
 \chi_u(z)=\frac{\psi(\rho_K(u) z)}u,\quad
 q_u(z)=-\Re\chi_u(z),\quad
 T(u)=\frac{\rho_K(u) H(\rho_K(u))}u,\quad \text{and}\quad 
 d(u)=\frac{\rho_K(u) D(\rho_K(u))}u.
\]
Since $P(t)/t\to\infty$, the same argument as in Lemma~\ref{lem:interval-escape} shows that, for all sufficiently large $u$, the first exit radius is finite and $\rho_K(u)=o(u)$, where $P(\rho_K(u))=Ku$. In particular, $\rho_K(u)>0$, and hence $|\chi_u(z)|\leqslant K$ for all $|z|\leqslant 1$ and $|\chi_u(1)|=K$. Applying Lemma~\ref{lem:smoothed} with frequency $\rho_K(u)$, gives
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:chi-estimates}
 \sup_{|z|\leqslant1}|\chi_u(z)-idz|\leqslant C_0T(u),
 \quad\text{and}\quad 
 \int_{-1}^1q_u(z)\,\mathrm{d} z\geqslant c_0T(u).
\end{equation}
Moreover, Lemma~\ref{lem:increment}, applied to $u$ and $\rho_K(u) z$, yields a $\widetilde E_u(z)$, such that
\[
 \psi(u+\rho_K(u) z)=\psi(u)+\psi(\rho_K(u) z)+\widetilde E_u(z),
 \quad \text{where} \quad 
 |\widetilde E_u(z)|
 \leqslant2\sqrt{Q(u)Q(\rho_K(u) z)}.
\]
Since $Q(\rho_K(u) z)=u q_u(z)$ and $Q(u)/u<\varepsilon$, division by $u$ implies the existence of a $E_u(z)$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:translated-chi}
 \frac{\psi(u+\rho_K(u) z)}u
 =
 \frac{\psi(u)}u+\chi_u(z)+E_u(z),
 \quad \text{where}\quad 
 |E_u(z)|\leqslant2\sqrt{\varepsilon q_u(z)}.
\end{equation}

Since $\rho_K(u)/u\to0$, we may take a constant $U>0$, and increase it so that, for all $u\geqslant U$ under consideration, we have
\begin{equation}\label{eq:large-u-average}
 u^{-1}\leqslant \frac{L}{256},
 \quad \text{and}\quad 
 \theta(u)\coloneqq\frac{\rho_K(u)}{u}
 \leqslant\min\left\{\frac1{10},\frac{L}{256R}\right\}.
\end{equation}
We use throughout the remainder of the proof $J_u=(u-\rho_K(u),u+\rho_K(u))$ and $r=\rho_K(u)/u$. By~\eqref{eq:large-u-average}, $r\leqslant 1/10$ and hence $J_u\subset(0,\infty)$. To prove~\eqref{eq:local-average}, it remains only to prove a uniform positive lower bound for the average of $\Phi_I$ over $J_u$. We will split in cases according to the size of $T(u)$.

\emph{Case 1.} Assume $T(u)\geqslant\delta$. Since $q_u(z)\geqslant0$, we have that $q_u(z)\leqslant|\chi_u(z)|\leqslant K$, and $\int_{-1}^1q_u(z)\,\mathrm{d} z\geqslant c_0 T(u)\geqslant c_0\delta$, where the set $ V=\{z\in[-1,1]: q_u(z)\geqslant c_0\delta/4\}$ has uniformly positive measure. Indeed,
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:V-case1-size}
c_0\delta
\leqslant \int_{-1}^1q_u(z)\,\mathrm{d} z
\leqslant K|V|+\frac{c_0\delta}{4}(2-|V|)
\leqslant K|V|+\frac{c_0\delta}{2},
\quad\text{implying}\quad
|V|\geqslant\frac{c_0\delta}{2K}>0.
\end{equation}

For $z\in V$, the lower bound in~\eqref{eq:Q-increment} together with the bound $\varepsilon\leqslant c_0\delta/16$, gives
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:bound_Q_rho_delta}
\frac{Q(u+\rho_K(u) z)}u
\geqslant
\big(\sqrt{q_u(z)}-\sqrt{Q(u)/u}\big)^2
\geqslant
\bigg(\sqrt{\frac{c_0\delta}{4}}-\sqrt{\varepsilon}\bigg)^2
\geqslant\frac{c_0\delta}{16}.
\end{equation}

We next obtain uniform upper bounds for $a(v)$ and $b(v)$ on the whole interval $J_u$. For $|z|\leqslant1$, the upper bound in~\eqref{eq:Q-increment}, together with $q_u(z)\leqslant K$, gives $Q(u+\rho_K(u) z)/u \leqslant(\sqrt{\varepsilon}+\sqrt K)^2$. Since $(u+\rho_K(u) z)/u=1+\theta(u) z\in[0.9,1.1]$, we obtain
\begin{equation}\label{eq:A_up_unif_bound}
    a(u+\rho_K(u) z)
 \leqslant
 \frac{1+(\sqrt\varepsilon+\sqrt K)^2}{0.9}.
\end{equation}
Similarly,~\eqref{eq:translated-chi}, $|\psi(u)|/u\leqslant M$, $|\chi_u(z)|\leqslant K$, and $q_u(z)\leqslant K$ imply
\begin{equation}\label{eq:b_up_unif_bound}
    |b(u+\rho_K(u) z)|
 \leqslant
 \frac{M+K+2\sqrt{\varepsilon K}}{0.9}.
\end{equation}
On the set $V$, the lower bound for $Q$ in~\eqref{eq:bound_Q_rho_delta} also gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:A_low_unif_bound}
     a(u+\rho_K(u) z)
 \geqslant
 \frac{Q(u+\rho_K(u) z)}{u+\rho_K(u) z}
 \geqslant\frac{c_0\delta}{20}.
\end{equation}
Consequently, there exists a constant $c_1>0$, depending only on $I,M,K,\delta$ and $c_0,C_0$, such that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Phi-case1-lower}
 \Phi_I(u+\rho_K(u) z)\geqslant c_1,
 \quad \text{for all } z\in V.
\end{equation}
Indeed, on $V$ the numerator $a(u+\rho_K(u) z)$ is uniformly bounded below as in~\eqref{eq:A_low_unif_bound}, whereas~\eqref{eq:A_up_unif_bound} and~\eqref{eq:b_up_unif_bound} implies that both $a(u+\rho_K(u) z)$ and $|b(u+\rho_K(u) z)|$ are uniformly bounded above.

Changing variables $w=u+\rho_K(u) z$ and using~\eqref{eq:V-case1-size}--\eqref{eq:Phi-case1-lower}, we obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \frac1{|J_u|}\int_{J_u}\Phi_I(w)\,\mathrm{d} w
 &=
 \frac12\int_{-1}^1\Phi_I(u+\rho_K(u) z)\,\mathrm{d} z \geqslant
 \frac{c_1|V|}{2}
 \geqslant
 \frac{c_1c_0\delta}{4K}>0.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus,~\eqref{eq:local-average} holds uniformly in this case.

\emph{Case 2.} Assume $T(u)<\delta$. The first estimate in~\eqref{eq:chi-estimates} now shows that $\chi_u$ is uniformly close to the purely imaginary linear function $z\mapsto idz$. Since $|\chi_u(1)|=K$, it follows that $||d(u)|-K| \leqslant|\chi_u(1)-id(u)| \leqslant C_0\delta$. By the choice $\delta\leqslant K/(4C_0)$, we may in particular use the coarser bounds $K/2\leqslant|d(u)|\leqslant 3K/2$. Moreover, because $idz$ is purely imaginary,
\[
 0\leqslant q_u(z)=-\Re\chi_u(z)
 \leqslant|\chi_u(z)-idz|
 \leqslant C_0\delta,
 \quad \text{for all } |z|\leqslant1.
\]

Put $b_0=B(u)/u$, so that $|b_0|\leqslant M$, and define
\[
 V= \{z \in \mathbb{R}:
 b_0+d(u)z\in
 [a+ L/4,b- L/4 ]\}.
\]
This is an interval of length $|V|=L/(2|d(u)|) \geqslant L/(3K)$. Note that $V \subset [-1,1]$, since if $z\in V$, then $|b_0+dz|\leqslant R$, and hence $|z| \leqslant (M+R)/|d(u)| \leqslant2(M+R)/K<1$ by the definition $K=4(M+R+1)$.

Fix $z\in V$ and write $w=u+\rho_K(u) z$. Taking imaginary parts in~\eqref{eq:translated-chi}, using $w/u=1+\theta(u) z$, and using the definitions in~\eqref{eq:delta-epsilon} and~\eqref{eq:large-u-average}, gives
\[
 |b(w)-(b_0+d(u)z)|
 \leqslant
 \frac{C_0\delta
       +2\sqrt{\varepsilon C_0\delta}
       +\theta(u) R}
      {1-\theta(u)} \leqslant \frac{L}{8}.
\]
Furthermore, the upper bound in~\eqref{eq:Q-increment} and $q_u(z)\leqslant C_0\delta$, together with~\eqref{eq:delta-epsilon} and~\eqref{eq:large-u-average}, yields
\[
 a(w)
 \leqslant
 \frac{u^{-1}
       +(\sqrt\varepsilon+\sqrt{C_0\delta})^2}
      {1-\theta(u)} \leqslant \frac{L}{8}.
\]
Since $b_0+d(u)z\in[a+L/4,b-L/4]$, it follows altogether that $b(w)-a\geqslant L/8$, $ b-b(w)\geqslant L/8$, and $ a(w)\leqslant L/8$. Using the explicit form of the integral in~\eqref{eq:Phi}, yields that 
\[
\Phi_I(w)
=\arctan\bigg(\frac{b-b(w)}{a(w)}\bigg)
+\arctan\bigg(\frac{b(w)-a}{a(w)}\bigg),
\]
and therefore each arctangent is at least $\arctan(1)=\pi/4$. Hence, $\Phi_I(u+\rho_K(u) z)\geqslant \pi/2$ for all $z \in V$. Changing variables $w=u+\rho_K(u)z$, then yields
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \frac1{|J_u|}\int_{J_u}\Phi_I(w)\,\mathrm{d} w
 &=
 \frac12\int_{-1}^1\Phi_I(u+\rho_K(u) z)\,\mathrm{d} z 
 \geqslant
 \frac{\pi}{4}|V|
 \geqslant
 \frac{\pi L}{12K}>0.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus,~\eqref{eq:local-average} also holds uniformly in Case~2.

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose $J_X(I)<\infty$ for one proper bounded interval $I$. We may and do assume without loss of generality that $\nu$ puts no mass on $\mathbb{R}\setminus(-1,1)$. By~\eqref{eq:occupation-equivalence} and~\eqref{eq:Fourier-identity}, $J_X(I)<\infty$ implies that $\int_0^\infty\Phi_I(u)u^{-1}\mathrm{d} u<\infty$. Lemma~\ref{lem:interval-escape} next gives $P(u)/u\to\infty$. 

Let $J$ be any other proper bounded interval. Choose $R\geqslant1$ such that $I\cup J\subset[-R,R]$, and set $M=2(R+1)$ and $E=\{u\geqslant1:\ |\psi(u)|\leqslant Mu\}$. Since $P(u)/u\to\infty$, Lemma~\ref{lem:local-average} applies with the interval $I$ and this value of $M$. Hence, there exist $c=c(I,M)>0$ and $U<\infty$ such that, for every $u\in E\cap[U,\infty)$, there exists $r\in(0,1/10]$ for which $\int_{(1-r)u}^{(1+r)u}\Phi_I(w)\,\mathrm{d} w\geqslant cru$. Applying Lemma~\ref{lem:covering} with $f=\Phi_I$ and $E\cap[U,\infty)$, we obtain $\int_{E\cap[U,\infty)}u^{-1}\mathrm{d} u<\infty$. The omitted portion $E\cap[1,U]$ has logarithmic measure at most $\log U<\infty$. Thus, 
\begin{equation}\label{eq:exceptional-frequency}
\int_{\{u\geqslant1:\,|\psi(u)|\leqslant Mu\}}\frac{\mathrm{d} u}{u}<\infty.
\end{equation}

We split the frequencies $u\geqslant1$ into $G=\{u\geqslant1:\ |\psi(u)|>Mu\}$ and $E=\{u\geqslant1:\ |\psi(u)|\leqslant Mu\}$. Consider first $u\in G$. For every $|r|\leqslant R$, $|1+iur| \leqslant 1+uR \leqslant u(R+1) =Mu/2 <|\psi(u)|/2$. The triangle inequality therefore gives $|\psi(u)|/2 \leqslant |1+iur-\psi(u)| \leqslant 3|\psi(u)|/2$. Since
\[
\Re\frac{1}{1+iur-\psi(u)}
=\frac{1+Q(u)}
{|1+iur-\psi(u)|^2},
\]
it follows that, uniformly in $|r|\leqslant R$, 
\[
\frac{4}{9}\frac{1+Q(u)}{|\psi(u)|^2}
\leqslant
\Re\frac{1}{1+iur-\psi(u)}
\leqslant
4\frac{1+Q(u)}{|\psi(u)|^2}.
\]
Integrating the upper bound over $J$ and the lower bound over $I$ gives $\Phi_J(u) \leqslant 4|J|(1+Q(u))/|\psi(u)|^2$ and $\Phi_I(u) \geqslant (4|I|/9)(1+Q(u))/|\psi(u)|^2$. Hence, $\Phi_J(u) \leqslant 9(|J|/|I|)\Phi_I(u)$ for all $u \in G$. Consequently,
\[
\int_{G}\Phi_J(u)\frac{\mathrm{d} u}{u}
\leqslant
9\frac{|J|}{|I|}
\int_1^\infty\Phi_I(u)\frac{\mathrm{d} u}{u}
<\infty.
\]

On the complementary set $E$, we use only the elementary bound and change of variables to obtain
\[
\Phi_J(u)
=
\int_J\frac{a(u)}
{a(u)^2+(r-b(u))^2}\,\mathrm{d} r
\leqslant
\int_{\mathbb{R}}\frac{a(u)}
{a(u)^2+(r-b(u))^2}\,\mathrm{d} r =
\int_{\mathbb{R}}\frac{\mathrm{d} y}{1+y^2}
=\pi.
\]
Together with~\eqref{eq:exceptional-frequency}, this yields
\[
\int_{E}\Phi_J(u)\frac{\mathrm{d} u}{u}
\leqslant
\pi\int_{E}\frac{\mathrm{d} u}{u}
<\infty.
\]
Combining the estimates on $G$ and $E$, we conclude that $\int_1^\infty\Phi_J(u)u^{-1}\mathrm{d} u<\infty$. The contribution from $0<u<1$ is finite by~\eqref{eq:small-frequency}. Thus, $\int_0^\infty\Phi_J(u)u^{-1} \mathrm{d} u <\infty$ and $J_X(J)<\infty$ by~\eqref{eq:Fourier-identity}. Since $J$ was arbitrary, finiteness of $J_X(I)$ for one proper bounded interval $I$ implies finiteness of $J_X(J)$ for every such $J$.

The equivalence with the abrupt/strongly-eroded dichotomy now follows from Vigon's abruptness criterion and the strong-erosion criterion recalled in Section~\ref{sec:introduction}, since $X$ is abrupt (resp. strongly eroded) if and only if $J_X(I)<\infty$ (resp. $J_X(I)=\infty$) for every proper bounded interval.

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $1-\cos z \geqslant z^2/4$ for $|z|\leqslant 1$ and $a_k u \leqslant 1$ for $u \in [a_n^{-1}, a_{n+1}^{-1}]$ and $k > n$,
\[
Q(u) \geqslant \lambda_n\bigl(1-\cos(a_n u)\bigr) + S_n u^2/4,
\quad\text{for all } u\in[a_n^{-1},a_{n+1}^{-1}].
\]
Partition $[a_n^{-1}, a_{n+1}^{-1}]$ into $J_n \coloneqq \lceil\log_2(a_n/a_{n+1})\rceil$ dyadic intervals $[y_{n,j}, z_{n,j}]$ with $y_{n,j} \coloneqq 2^{j-1} a_n^{-1}$ and $z_{n,j} \coloneqq \min\{2y_{n,j}, a_{n+1}^{-1}\}$. Then $u + S_n u^2/4 \geqslant q_{n,j} \coloneqq y_{n,j} + S_n y_{n,j}^2/4$ for $u \in [y_{n,j}, z_{n,j}]$. Covering each dyadic subinterval by at most $K_{n,j} \coloneqq \lceil y_{n,j}/P_n\rceil$ full periods of length $P_n = 2\pi/ a_n$ (noting that $K_{n,j}P_n \leqslant (1+2\pi)y_{n,j}\leqslant 8y_{n,j}$) and applying Lemma~\ref{lem:periodic} yields
\[
\int_{y_{n,j}}^{z_{n,j}} \frac{\mathrm{d} u}{u + Q(u)} 
\leqslant \sum_{k=1}^{K_{n,j}}\int_{y_{n,j}+(k-1)P_n}^{y_{n,j}+kP_n}\frac{\mathrm{d} u}{q_{n,j} + \lambda_n(1-\cos(a_n u))}
\leqslant 8\rho_{n,j},
\quad
\rho_{n,j}\coloneqq\frac{y_{n,j}}{\sqrt{q_{n,j}(q_{n,j} + 2\lambda_n)}}.
\]

Partition $\mathcal{J}_n = \{1, \dots, J_n\}$ into the sets
\[
\mathcal{J}_n^1 = \{j \in \mathcal{J}_n : S_n y_{n,j} \leqslant 4\}, 
\quad \mathcal{J}_n^2 = \{j \in \mathcal{J}_n : S_n y_{n,j} \in(4,2h_n]\}, 
\quad \mathcal{J}_n^3 = \{j \in \mathcal{J}_n : S_ny_{n,j} > 2h_n\}.
\]
Using $q_{n,j} \geqslant y_{n,j}$ on $\mathcal{J}_n^1$, $4q_{n,j} \geqslant S_n y_{n,j}^2$ on $\mathcal{J}_n^2$ and $\mathcal{J}_n^3$, and $q_{n,j} + 2\lambda_n \geqslant 2\lambda_n$ on $\mathcal{J}_n^1$ and $\mathcal{J}_n^2$, we obtain:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},leftmargin=2em]
\item For $j \in \mathcal{J}_n^1$, we have $\rho_{n,j} \leqslant \sqrt{y_{n,j}/(2\lambda_n)}$. Summing backwards from $j_{\max} \coloneqq \sup \mathcal{J}_n^1$ yields 
\[
\sum_{j\in\mathcal{J}_n^1} \rho_{n,j} 
\leqslant \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\lambda_nS_n}}\sum_{k\geqslant 0} \sqrt{2^{-k}S_n y_{n,j_{\max}}}
\leqslant\frac{2}{\sqrt{2\lambda_n S_n}(1 - 2^{-1/2})} 
\leqslant \frac{5}{h_n}.
\]
\item For $j \in \mathcal{J}_n^2$, we have $\rho_{n,j} \leqslant \sqrt{2/\lambda_n S_n} = \sqrt{2}/h_n$. Since $|\mathcal{J}_n^2| \leqslant 0\vee\lceil \log_2 h_n-1 \rceil \leqslant \log_2(h_n\vee1)$, 
\[
\sum_{j\in\mathcal{J}_n^2} \rho_{n,j}
\leqslant\frac{\sqrt{2}\log_2(h_n \vee 1)}{h_n}
\leqslant\frac{\sqrt{8}\log(h_n \vee 1)}{h_n}.
\]
\item For $j \in \mathcal{J}_n^3$, we have $\rho_{n,j} \leqslant 4/(S_n y_{n,j})$. Summing forwards from $j_{\min} = \inf \mathcal{J}_n^3$ yields 
\[
\sum_{j\in\mathcal{J}_n^3} \rho_{n,j}
\leqslant\sum_{k\geqslant 0} \frac{4}{2^kS_ny_{n,j_{\min}}}
=\frac{8}{S_ny_{n,j_{\min}}}
\leqslant \frac{4}{h_n}.
\]
\end{enumerate}
Adding these three bounds over $n\geqslant 1$, we find that
\[
\mathfrak{z}_0
\leqslant\int_1^{a_1^{-1}}\frac{\mathrm{d} u}{u}+\sum_{n\geqslant 1}\int_{a_n^{-1}}^{a_{n+1}^{-1}} \frac{\mathrm{d} u}{u + Q(u)} 
\leqslant -\log a_1 + 72\sum_{n\geqslant 1}\frac{1 + \log(h_n \vee 1)}{h_n}.
\]
An application of Lemma~\ref{lem:z1}(i) shows that $\mathfrak{s}_1 \in L^1_\mathrm{loc}(\mathbb{R})$, making $X$ abrupt.

body_md:
\textbf{Part (i).} From~\eqref{eq:general-QB}, $\sum_{k\leqslant n} \Delta_ka_k^{-1} (\sin(a_ku)-a_ku) = \sum_{k\leqslant n} \Delta_ka_k^{-1}\sin(a_ku) +d_nu$. Using next, that $|\Delta_k|\leqslant1$, $|\sin z|\leqslant1$, and $|\sin z-z|\leqslant |z|^3/6$, we obtain for all $u>0$ and $n \geqslant 1$, that
\[
|B(u)-d_nu|
\leqslant
\sum_{k\leqslant n}a_k^{-1}
+\frac{u^3}{6}\sum_{k>n}a_k^2
\leqslant
2a_n^{-1}
+\frac13a_{n+1}^2u^3,
\]
since $a_k/a_{k-1}\leqslant a_{k-1}\leqslant1/2$ and
$(a_{k+1}/a_k)^2\leqslant a_k^2\leqslant1/4$.

\noindent\textbf{Part (ii).} Fix $n\geqslant1$ and $u\geqslant a_n^{-1}$. We split
\[
1+Q(u)
=
1+\sum_{k<n}\lambda_k\bigl(1-\cos(a_ku)\bigr)
+
\lambda_n\bigl(1-\cos(a_nu)\bigr)
+
\sum_{k>n}\lambda_k\bigl(1-\cos(a_ku)\bigr).
\]
For the sum over $k<n$, the bound $1-\cos z\leqslant2$ gives $1+\sum_{k<n}\lambda_k(1-\cos(a_ku))\leqslant 1+2L_{n-1}$. Assumption~\eqref{eq:drift-resonance-head-tail} then gives $1+\sum_{k<n}\lambda_k(1-\cos(a_ku)) \leqslant C v_{n+1}u^2$ for $u\geqslant a_n^{-1}$. For the sum over $k>n$, the quadratic estimate $1-\cos z\leqslant z^2/2$ and~\eqref{eq:drift-resonance-head-tail} give
\begin{equation*}
    \sum_{k>n}\lambda_k\bigl(1-\cos(a_ku)\bigr) \leqslant
\frac{u^2}{2}\sum_{k>n}\lambda_k a_k^2 =
\frac{u^2}{2}S_n \leqslant
\frac{C}{2}v_{n+1}u^2.
\end{equation*}
Combining the estimates, we obtain~\eqref{eq:Q-upper-tail}.

\noindent\textbf{Part (iii).} For $u\geqslant W_n$, we have $2a_n^{-1} = v_{n+1}W_n^2/8 \leqslant v_{n+1}u^2/8$. On the other hand, for $u\leqslant v_{n+1}^{-1}$, it holds that $a_{n+1}^2u^3/3 \leqslant a_{n+1}^2u^2/(3v_{n+1}) \leqslant v_{n+1}u^2/8$ for all sufficiently large $n$, by $v_{n+1}/a_{n+1}\to\infty$. Hence, $|B(u)-d_nu|\leqslant v_{n+1}u^2/4$. The same assumption implies that $a_{n+1}/v_{n+1}\leqslant1$ for all sufficiently large $n$. Thus, for $u\in I_n=[W_n,v_{n+1}^{-1}]$, the $(n+1)$-th summand in $Q$ and the inequality $1-\cos z\geqslant z^2/4$ for $|z|\leqslant1$ give the first part of~\eqref{eq:drift-resonance-BQ}: \[
Q(u)
\geqslant
\lambda_{n+1}\bigl(1-\cos(a_{n+1}u)\bigr)
\geqslant \frac{1}{4}\lambda_{n+1}a_{n+1}^2u^2 
=\frac{1}{4} v_{n+1}u^2
\geqslant 
|B(u)-d_nu|.
\]

It remains to estimate $\mathfrak{z}(I_n)$. Set $P_n=2\pi a_n^{-1}$. On every complete period $[jP_n,(j+1)P_n]\subset[W_n,v_{n+1}^{-1}]$, Part~(ii) gives $1+Q(u) \leqslant \lambda_n(1-\cos(a_nu))+q_j$ for $q_j \coloneqq (3C/2)v_{n+1}((j+1)P_n)^2$. Since $(j+1)P_n\leqslant v_{n+1}^{-1}$, it follows that $q_j \leqslant 3C/(2v_{n+1}) \leqslant \lambda_n$ for all sufficiently large $n$, since $\lambda_nv_{n+1}\to\infty$. Hence, Lemma~\ref{lem:periodic} together with $S_n\geqslant v_{n+1}$ and $h_n=\sqrt{\lambda_nS_n}\geqslant\sqrt{\lambda_nv_{n+1}}$, yields
\begin{align*}
\int_{jP_n}^{(j+1)P_n}\frac{\mathrm{d} u}{1+Q(u)}
&\geqslant
\frac{P_n}{\sqrt{q_j(q_j+2\lambda_n)}} \geqslant
\frac{P_n}{\sqrt{3\lambda_nq_j}} =
\frac{1}{\sqrt{3(3C/2)\lambda_nv_{n+1}}}
\frac{1}{j+1}\\
&=
\frac{1}{3}\sqrt{\frac{2}{C}}\,
\frac{1}{\sqrt{\lambda_nv_{n+1}}}
\frac{1}{j+1}\geqslant
\frac{1}{3h_n}\sqrt{\frac{2}{C}}
\frac{1}{j+1}.
\end{align*}

Finally, let $j_0=\lceil W_n/P_n\rceil$, and $j_1=\lfloor(v_{n+1}P_n)^{-1}\rfloor-1$. Whenever the right-hand side below is positive, it follows that
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{j=j_0}^{j_1}\frac1{j+1}
&\geqslant
\log\biggl(\frac{j_1+2}{j_0+1}\biggr) 
\geqslant
\log\biggl(\frac{v_{n+1}^{-1}}{W_n+2P_n}\biggr) 
\geqslant
\log\biggl(\frac{v_{n+1}^{-1}}{W_n}\biggr)-\log(1+4\pi)
\geqslant
\log\biggl(\frac{v_{n+1}^{-1}}{W_n}\biggr)-2\pi,
\end{aligned}
\]
where we used $W_n\geqslant a_n^{-1}$ and hence $P_n=2\pi a_n^{-1}\leqslant2\pi W_n$. If the right-hand side is non-positive, the desired lower bound is trivial. Summing the preceding period estimates proves~\eqref{eq:drift-resonance-BQ}.

\begin{equation*}

\sum_{n\geqslant1}n^2 2^{-2^{n+1}/3}
<\infty, \quad \text{while}\quad 
\lambda_n a_n
=
n^2 a_n^{-1/3}
=
n^2 2^{2^n/3}\to\infty,
\end{equation*} as $n \to \infty$. Thus, $\nu$ is a valid L\'evy measure and the corresponding process has infinite variation. Moreover, $\nu$ is symmetric and $B(u) \equiv 0$, so $b(u) \equiv 0$.

Recall that $v_n=\lambda_na_n^2$. Since $a_{n+1}=a_n^2$, it follows that $v_n=n^2a_n^{2/3}$, and $v_{n+1}=(n+1)^2a_n^{4/3}$. Moreover, $v_{k+1}/v_k\leqslant1/2$ for all sufficiently large $k$, and therefore $v_{n+1}\leqslant S_n\leqslant2v_{n+1}$. Consequently, $n(n+1) = \sqrt{\lambda_nv_{n+1}} \leqslant h_n \leqslant \sqrt{2\lambda_nv_{n+1}} = \sqrt2\,n(n+1)$, implying that $\sum_{n\geqslant1} (1+\log(h_n\vee1))/h_n <\infty$. Proposition~\ref{prop:abstract-Iplus} therefore gives $\mathfrak{z}_0<\infty$, and Lemma~\ref{lem:z1}(i) yields $\mathfrak{s}_1\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb{R})$, so $X$ is abrupt.

We next prove that $\mathfrak{s}_1(0)=\infty$. We verify the hypotheses of Proposition~\ref{prop:abstract-drift-resonance}(iii) with $C=4$. We already have $S_n\leqslant2v_{n+1}\leqslant4v_{n+1}$. Furthermore, $\lambda_{k-1}/\lambda_k \to 0$ such that $L_{n-1}\leqslant2\lambda_{n-1}$ for all sufficiently large $n$. Since $a_n=a_{n-1}^2$, we have $\lambda_{n-1} = (n-1)^2a_n^{-2/3}$, and hence
\[
1+2L_{n-1}
\leqslant
1+4(n-1)^2a_n^{-2/3}
\leqslant
4(n+1)^2a_n^{-2/3}
=
4v_{n+1}a_n^{-2}, 
\]
for all sufficiently large $n$. Moreover, $v_{n+1}/a_{n+1} = (n+1)^2a_n^{-2/3} \to\infty$, and $\lambda_nv_{n+1} = n^2(n+1)^2 \to\infty$. For $W_n=4/\sqrt{a_nv_{n+1}}$, it follows that $W_n a_n = 4 a_n^{-1/6}/(n+1) \to\infty$, and $a_{n+1}/v_{n+1} \to0$, implying for all sufficiently large $n$, that $I_n\coloneqq[W_n,v_{n+1}^{-1}] \subset[a_n^{-1},a_{n+1}^{-1}]$. Proposition~\ref{prop:abstract-drift-resonance}(iii), with $C=4$, therefore gives
\[
\mathfrak{z}(I_n)
\geqslant
\frac{1}{3\sqrt2\,h_n}
\left(
\log\mleft(\frac{v_{n+1}^{-1}}{W_n}\mright)-2\pi
\right)=\frac{1}{3\sqrt2\,h_n}
\left(
\frac{2^n\log2}{6}
-\log(4(n+1))-2\pi
\right).
\]
Together with $h_n\leqslant\sqrt2\,n(n+1)$, this implies that, for some $c>0$ and all sufficiently large $n$, that $\mathfrak{z}(I_n) \geqslant c 2^n/n^2 \to\infty$. Hence, for $I=\bigcup_{n\geqslant1}I_n$, we have $\mathfrak{z}(I)=\infty$. Since $B\equiv0$, $\sup_{u\in I} |B(u)|/(1+Q(u)) =0$, and Lemma~\ref{lem:z1}(iii) yields $\mathfrak{s}_1(0)=\infty$.

Finally, fix $r\neq0$. Since $b(u)\equiv0$, taking $\delta=|r|/2$ gives $E_\delta \coloneqq \{u\geqslant1:|r-b(u)|<\delta\} = \emptyset$. Thus, $\mathfrak{z}(E_\delta)=0$, while $\mathfrak{z}_0<\infty$. Lemma~\ref{lem:z1}(ii) therefore implies that $\mathfrak{s}_1(r)<\infty$, for all $r \ne 0$.

body_md:
\noindent\textbf{Step 1. The L\'evy measure.} Define the set and constants
\[
C=\Biggl\{\sum_{j\geqslant1}\varepsilon_j\tau_j:
(\varepsilon_j)_{j\geqslant 1}\in\{0,1\}^\mathbb{N}\Biggr\},
\quad
\text{where}
\quad
\tau_j\coloneqq\exp\bigl(-4^{2^j}\bigr),
\quad \text{for all }j\geqslant 1.
\]
Writing $R_j=\sum_{k>j}\tau_k$, we have $\tau_{j+1}\leqslant R_j\leqslant2\tau_{j+1}$, and $\tau_j>R_j$ for all $j \geqslant 1$. Consequently, the binary expansions defining $C$ are unique, making $C$ uncountable. Moreover, $C$ is covered by $2^j$ intervals of length $R_j$. Since $2^jR_j\to0$, the Lebesgue measure of $C$ is zero. Each sum $\sum_{j\geqslant 1}\varepsilon_j\tau_j$ can be approximated with the corresponding sum of $(\varepsilon_{j}+(1-2\varepsilon_k)\1_{\{j=k\}} )_{j\geqslant 1}\ne(\varepsilon_j)_{j\geqslant 1}$ as $k\to\infty$. Thus, $C\subset[0,1]$ is perfect and compact.

For each $j\geqslant0$, let $(d_n)_{2^j\leqslant n<2^{j+1}}$ enumerate, in lexicographic order, the $2^j$ partial sums $\sum_{k\leqslant j}\varepsilon_k\tau_k$ over every finite sequence $(\varepsilon_k)_{k\leqslant j}\in\{0,1\}^j$. The empty sum gives $d_1=0$. Set $d_0\coloneqq 0$ and $\Delta_n\coloneqq d_{n-1}-d_n$. Since $d_n\in C\subset[0,1]$, we have $|\Delta_n|\leqslant1$.

Let $X$ have zero Gaussian coefficient, zero drift parameter and L\'evy measure as in~\eqref{eq:general-lacunary-nu}: 
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:cantor-levy-measure}
\nu=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{n\geqslant1}
\bigg[
\bigg(\lambda_n+\frac{\Delta_n}{a_n}\bigg)\delta_{a_n}
+
\bigg(\lambda_n-\frac{\Delta_n}{a_n}\bigg)\delta_{-a_n}
\bigg],
\quad\text{where}\quad
a_n=2^{-n}e^{-(5/2)4^n},
\enskip
\lambda_n=4^ne^{4^{n+1}}.
\end{equation}
All coefficients are positive because $\lambda_na_n>1$. Furthermore,
\[
\int_{\mathbb{R}}x^2\nu(\mathrm{d} x)
=\sum_{n\geqslant1}\lambda_na_n^2
=\sum_{n\geqslant1}e^{-4^n}<\infty,
\quad \text{and}\quad 
\int_{\mathbb{R}}|x|\nu(\mathrm{d} x)
=\sum_{n\geqslant1}\lambda_na_n
=\sum_{n\geqslant1}2^ne^{(3/2)4^n}=\infty.
\]
Thus,~\eqref{eq:cantor-levy-measure} specifies an infinite-variation L\'evy process with finite variance.

\noindent\textbf{Step 2. Establishing $\mathfrak{z}_0<\infty$.} 
Recall $v_n=\lambda_na_n^2=\exp(-4^n)$ and note that $\sqrt{\lambda_nv_{n+1}}=2^n$ for $n\geqslant 1$. Then $v_{n+1}\leqslant v_n/2$, which gives $v_{n+1}\leqslant S_n\leqslant 2v_{n+1}$ and $1\leqslant 2^n\leqslant h_n=\sqrt{\lambda_nS_n}\leqslant 2^{n+1/2}$. Thus, 
\[
\sum_{n\geqslant 1}\frac{1+\log h_n}{h_n}
\leqslant \sum_{n\geqslant 1}(n+3/2)2^{-n}<\infty.
\]
Proposition~\ref{prop:abstract-Iplus} implies that $\mathfrak{z}_0<\infty$, making $X$ abrupt and $\mathfrak{s}_1\in L^1_\mathrm{loc}(\mathbb{R})$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:z1}.

\noindent\textbf{Step 3. Divergence estimate.} We will show that the assumptions of Proposition~\ref{prop:abstract-drift-resonance}(ii)~\&~(iii) hold. We have already established that $S_n\leqslant 2v_{n+1}$. Moreover, 
\[
1+2L_{n-1}
=1+2\sum_{k\leqslant n-1}4^ke^{4^{k+1}}
\leqslant 4^ne^{4^n}
= v_{n+1}a_n^{-2}.
\]
Thus,~\eqref{eq:drift-resonance-head-tail} holds with $C=2$. Next, recall $W_n\coloneqq 4/\sqrt{a_nv_{n+1}}$ and note that
\[
a_n^{-1}
\leqslant W_n
=2^{2+n/2}e^{13\cdot 4^{n-1}}
\leqslant v_{n+1}^{-1}
= 2^{-n-1}e^{-(3/2)4^{n+1}}a_{n+1}^{-1}
\leqslant a_{n+1}^{-1}.
\]
Thus, $I_n\coloneqq[W_n,v_{n+1}^{-1}]\subset[a^{-1}_n,a^{-1}_{n+1}]$, as required by Proposition~\ref{prop:abstract-drift-resonance}(iii). Since $h_n\leqslant 2^{n+1/2}$ and $v_{n+1}W_n=2^{2+n/2}\exp(-3\cdot 4^{n-1})$, Proposition~\ref{prop:abstract-drift-resonance}(ii)~\&~(iii) yields, for all sufficiently large $n$,
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:cantor-drift-estimate-2}
\mathfrak{z}(I_n)
\geqslant \frac{2^{-n}}{3\sqrt{2}}\bigl(
3\cdot 4^{n-1}-(2+n/2)\log 2-2\pi
\bigr)
\quad\text{and}\quad
|B(u)-d_nu|
\leqslant \frac{1}{4}v_{n+1}u^2
\leqslant Q(u),
\quad
\text{for}\enskip
u\in I_n.
\end{equation}
In particular, $\mathfrak{z}(I_n)\to\infty$ as $n\to\infty$. Moreover, if $|r-d_n|\leqslant v_n$, then for all sufficiently large $n$,
\[
|r-d_n|
\leqslant v_n
=2^{-2-n/2}v_{n-1}\cdot v_{n+1}W_n
\leqslant v_{n+1}W_n/4
\leqslant v_{n+1}u/4,
\quad
\text{for}\enskip
u\in I_n.
\]
Together with~\eqref{eq:cantor-drift-estimate-2}, this gives 
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:cantor-kernel-lower}
|ru-B(u)|\leqslant2Q(u),
\quad\text{for all sufficiently large $n$ whenever}\quad
|r-d_n|\leqslant v_n
\quad\text{and}\quad
u\in I_n.
\end{equation}

\noindent\textbf{Step 4. Divergence for $r \in C$.}
Fix $r \in C$, so $r = \sum_{k=1}^\infty \varepsilon_k \tau_k$ and recall $R_j=\sum_{k>j}\tau_k$. For each~$j$, the truncation $\sum_{k=1}^j \varepsilon_k \tau_k$ equals some $d_{n_j}$ with $2^j \leqslant n_j < 2^{j+1}$. Because $n_j \leqslant 2^{j+1}-1$,
\[
|r - d_{n_j}| \leqslant R_j \leqslant 2\tau_{j+1} = 2 \exp(-4^{2^{j+1}}) 
\leqslant \exp(-4^{n_j})
=v_{n_j}.
\]
Setting $I \coloneqq \bigcup_{j\geqslant j_0} I_{n_j}$ for some sufficiently large~$j_0$, we get $\mathfrak{z}(I) = \infty$ because $\mathfrak{z}(I_{n_j}) \to \infty$ as $j\to\infty$ by~\eqref{eq:cantor-drift-estimate-2}. By~\eqref{eq:cantor-kernel-lower}, $\sup_{u\in I} |B(u)-ru|/(1+Q(u)) \leqslant 2$, so Lemma~\ref{lem:z1}(iii) then gives $\mathfrak{s}_1(r) = \infty$.

\noindent\textbf{Step 5. Finiteness for $r \notin C$.}
Fix $r \notin C$ and set $\delta \coloneqq \operatorname{dist}(r, C)/2 > 0$. On the intervals $\tilde I_n \coloneqq [2^n a_n^{-1}, 2^{-(n+1)}a^{-1}_{n+1}]$, Inequality~\eqref{eq:B-drift-tracking} gives
\[
\sup_{u\in \tilde I_n} |b(u) - d_n| 
\leqslant 2^{1-n} 
+ 4^{-n-1}/3
\to 0.
\]
Since $d_n \in C$, we have $|r - d_n| \geqslant 2\delta$. Thus, for all sufficiently large $n$ and $u\in \tilde I_n$, we have $|b(u) - d_n| < \delta$ and hence $|r - b(u)| \geqslant \delta$. Thus, the set $E \coloneqq \{u \geqslant 1 : |r - b(u)| < \delta\}$ intersects $\tilde I_n$ for only finitely many $n$, and is contained in the union of the intervals $J_n \coloneqq [2^{-n} a_n^{-1}, 2^n a_n^{-1}]$ together with the finitely many intervals $\tilde I_n$ that it does intersect. Since $\mathfrak{z}_0 < \infty$, Lemma~\ref{lem:z1}(ii) will imply that $\mathfrak{s}_1(r) < \infty$ as soon as we show that $\sum_{n\geqslant 1}\mathfrak{z}(J_n)<\infty$, which would complete the proof. In fact, it suffices to show that $\sum_{n\geqslant 1}\mathfrak{z}(J_n^l)$ for $l\in\{1,2\}$, where $J_n^1\coloneqq[2^{-n} a_n^{-1}, a_n^{-1}]$ and $J_n^2\coloneqq[a_n^{-1}, 2^n a_n^{-1}]$.

Let us bound $\mathfrak{z}(J_n^1)$. For $u\in J_n^1=[2^{-n} a_n^{-1}, a_n^{-1}]$, the bound $1-\cos z\geqslant z^2/4$ for $|z|\leqslant 1$ yields
\[
1+Q(u)
\geqslant
\lambda_{n}\bigl(1-\cos(a_{n}u)\bigr)
\geqslant \frac{1}{4}\lambda_{n}a_{n}^2u^2 
=\frac{1}{4} v_{n}u^2
\geqslant \frac{1}{4} 4^{-n} \lambda_n.
\]
Thus, we have the summable upper bound
\[
\sum_{n\geqslant 1}\mathfrak{z}(J_n^1)
=\sum_{n\geqslant 1}\int_{J_n^1} \frac{\mathrm{d} u}{1+Q(u)} 
\leqslant \sum_{n\geqslant 1}\frac{4\cdot 4^n}{\lambda_n a_n} 
= \sum_{n\geqslant 1}4\cdot 2^n e^{-(3/2)4^n}
<\infty.
\]

For $u\in J_n^2=[a_n^{-1}, 2^n a_n^{-1}]$, we have $u\leqslant 2^na_n^{-1}\leqslant a_{n+1}^{-1}$. The bound $1-\cos z\geqslant z^2/4$ for $|z|\leqslant 1$ gives
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:step5-Q-lower}
1+Q(u) 
\geqslant \lambda_n(1-\cos(a_nu))
+\lambda_{n+1}(1-\cos(a_{n+1}u))
\geqslant \lambda_n(1-\cos(a_nu))+\frac{1}{4}v_{n+1}u^2,
\quad u\in J_n^2.
\end{equation}
Partition the interval $[a_n^{-1}, 2^n a_n^{-1}]$ into $[ja_n^{-1},(j+1)a_n^{-1}]$ for $j\in\{1,\ldots,2^n\}$. For $u\in [ja_n^{-1},(j+1)a_n^{-1}]$, 
\[
\frac{1}{4} v_{n+1} u^2 
\geqslant \frac{1}{4} j^2 v_{n+1}a_n^{-2} 
\eqqcolon q_j.
\]
Using~\eqref{eq:step5-Q-lower} and applying Lemma~\ref{lem:periodic} yields:
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:step5-single-period}
\int_{ja_n^{-1}}^{(j+1)a_n^{-1}} \frac{\mathrm{d} u}{1 + Q(u)} 
\leqslant \int_{ja_n^{-1}}^{ja_n^{-1}+2\pi a_n^{-1}} \frac{\mathrm{d} u}{q_j + \lambda_n \bigl(1 - \cos(a_n u)\bigr)} 
=\frac{2\pi a_n^{-1}}{\sqrt{q_j (q_j + 2\lambda_n)}}.
\end{equation}
Since $q_j + 2\lambda_n \geqslant 2\lambda_n$, we get $\sqrt{q_j (q_j + 2\lambda_n)} \geqslant \sqrt{2 \lambda_n q_j}$, so the upper bound in~\eqref{eq:step5-single-period} satisfies
\[
\frac{2\pi a_n^{-1}}{\sqrt{q_j (q_j + 2\lambda_n)}} 
\leqslant \frac{2\sqrt{2}\pi a_n^{-1}}{\sqrt{j^2\lambda_nv_{n+1}a_n^{-2}}} = \frac{2\sqrt{2}\pi}{j \sqrt{\lambda_n v_{n+1}}} 
= \frac{2\sqrt{2}\pi}{j 2^n}
\leqslant \frac{9}{j 2^n}.
\]
Combining this bound with~\eqref{eq:step5-single-period} and summing over $1\leqslant j\leqslant 2^n$ and $n\geqslant 1$, we obtain 
\[
\sum_{n\geqslant 1}\mathfrak{z}(J_n^2)
=\sum_{n\geqslant 1}\int_{J_n^2} \frac{\mathrm{d} u}{1 + Q(u)}
\leqslant
\sum_{n\geqslant 1}\sum_{j=1}^{2^n} \int_{ja_n^{-1}}^{(j+1)a_n^{-1}} \!\!\!\frac{\mathrm{d} u}{1 + Q(u)}
\leqslant \sum_{n\geqslant 1}\sum_{j=1}^{2^n} \frac{9}{j 2^n} 
\leqslant 9\sum_{n\geqslant 1}\frac{1+n\log 2}{2^n}<\infty.\qedhere
\]

body_md:
First assume $\psi$ is as in~\eqref{eq:compact-exponent} (i.e., $\nu$ is supported on $(-1,1)$), and let $H,D$ be as in~\eqref{eq:HD}. Put
\[
\mathcal E
\coloneqq
\int_1^\infty
\frac{Q(u)}
{u^2\bigl(1+H(u)^2+D(u)^2\bigr)}\,\mathrm{d} u.
\]
By~\eqref{eq:dyadic-HD} and the elementary inequalities $(a+b)^2\leqslant 2(a^2+b^2)$ and $2(2\log 2)^2\leqslant 4$, we have
\[
1+H(w)^2+D(w)^2
\leqslant
8\bigl(1+H(u)^2+D(u)^2\bigr),
\quad\text{for}\enskip
u\leqslant w\leqslant 2u.
\]
Since $w^{-2}\geqslant(4u^2)^{-1}$ on $[u,2u]$, the second estimate in~\eqref{eq:smoothed-average}, after the change of variables $w=uz$, gives
\[
\int_u^{2u}
\frac{Q(w)}
{w^2\bigl(1+H(w)^2+D(w)^2\bigr)}\,\mathrm{d} w
\geqslant
\frac{\int_u^{2u}Q(w)\,\mathrm{d} w}{32u^2\bigl(1+H(u)^2+D(u)^2\bigr)}
\geqslant
\frac{c_0H(u)}
{32\bigl(1+H(u)^2+D(u)^2\bigr)}.
\]
Integrating this inequality against $u^{-1}\mathrm{d} u$ and applying Tonelli's theorem yields the following estimate: after interchanging the two integrals, a fixed $w$ is counted only for $u\in[w/2,w]\cap[1,\infty)$, whose $u^{-1}\mathrm{d} u$-measure is at most $\log2$. Hence,
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:bounded-envelope-energy}
\int_1^\infty
\frac{H(u)}{1+H(u)^2+D(u)^2}\frac{\mathrm{d} u}{u}
\leqslant
\frac{32\log2}{c_0}\mathcal E.
\end{equation}
If $\mathcal E<\infty$, then~\eqref{eq:bounded-envelope-energy} and Lemma~\ref{lem:energy-escape} would imply $P(u)/u\to\infty$, contradicting~\eqref{eq:bounded-envelope}. Thus, $\mathcal E=\infty$.

Next,~\eqref{eq:smoothed-approximation} at $z=1$ gives $|\psi(u)-iuD(u)|\leqslant C_0uH(u)$. For $u\geqslant1$, this implies
\[
 |1+iur-\psi(u)|^2
 \leqslant
 100(1+r^2)u^2\bigl(1+H(u)^2+D(u)^2\bigr).
\]
Since $1+Q(u)\geqslant Q(u)$ and $\psi(-u)=\overline{\psi(u)}$, we see that $\mathfrak{s}_1(r)
\geqslant
(100\pi(1+r^2))^{-1}\mathcal E
=\infty$.

For a general L\'evy measure, let $\psi_0$ be the characteristic exponent obtained by removing the jumps on $\mathbb{R}\setminus(-1,1)$, keeping the Gaussian coefficient and drift parameter. Then,
\[
 \psi(u)-\psi_0(u)
 =
 \int_{\mathbb{R}\setminus(-1,1)}(e^{iux}-1)\nu(\mathrm{d} x),
 \quad \text{and}\quad 
 |\psi(u)-\psi_0(u)|
 \leqslant M_0 \coloneqq 2\nu(\mathbb{R}\setminus(-1,1))<\infty.
\]
The truncated process also has infinite variation and $P_0(u)\coloneqq\sup_{0\leqslant v\leqslant u}|\psi_0(v)|\leqslant P(u)+M_0$, so~\eqref{eq:bounded-envelope} also holds for $P_0$. The corresponding function to $\mathfrak{s}_{1}$ is identically infinite. If $z=1+iur-\psi(u)$ and $z_0=1+iur-\psi_0(u)$, then $|z_0|\geqslant1$, $|z|\leqslant(1+M_0)|z_0|$, and $\Re z\geqslant\Re z_0$. Consequently, $\Re(z^{-1})\geqslant(1+M_0)^{-2}\Re(z_0^{-1})$. Integration gives $\mathfrak{s}_1(r)=\infty$ for all $r\in\mathbb{R}$.

Recall $\nu = c\sum_{n\geqslant1}b_n^{-\alpha} (\delta_{b_n}+\delta_{-b_n})$ with $b_n=2^{-\eta^n}$ and $\eta(2-\alpha)>2>\alpha$. Since $b_{n+1} = b_n^\eta$, geometric comparisons give $\sum_{k\leqslant n} b_k^{-\alpha} \leqslant C_1 b_n^{-\alpha}$ and $\sum_{k>n} b_k^{2-\alpha} \leqslant C_2 b_{n+1}^{2-\alpha}$, showing that $\nu$ has a finite second moment. 

Set $r_n = 2b_n$ and $t_n = 2cb_n^{2-\alpha}$. Symmetry gives $d(r_n) = 0$. Since $b_{n+1} \leqslant b_n/4$, the cutoff isolates the scales: $V(r_n) = 2c\sum_{k\geqslant n} b_k^{2-\alpha}$ and $\overline{\nu}(r_n) = 2c\sum_{k<n} b_k^{-\alpha}$. As $n \to \infty$, it therefore follows that
\[
\frac{r_n}{t_n} = \frac{b_n^{\alpha-1}}{c} \to 0, 
\quad
1\leqslant \frac{V(r_n)}{t_n} \leqslant 1 + C_2 b_n^{(\eta-1)(2-\alpha)}\to 1, 
\quad \text{and} \quad
t_n \overline{\nu}(r_n) \leqslant 4c^2 C_1 b_{n-1}^{\eta(2-\alpha)-\alpha} \to 0.
\]
Proposition~\ref{prop:gen-Gaussian} implies that $X$ is strongly eroded and $\mathfrak{s}_{1} \equiv \infty$.

For the activity indices, $\int_{(-1,1)} |x|^p \nu(\mathrm{d} x) = 2c\sum_{n\geqslant 1} b_n^{p-\alpha}$ converges if and only if $p > \alpha$, giving $\beta_+ = \alpha$. To see that $\beta_- = 0$, note that $\eta(2-\alpha) > 2$ and the strict cutoff in $V(b_n)$ excludes $\pm b_n$, so
\[
b_n^{p-2} V(b_n) = 2c b_n^{p-2} \sum_{k>n} b_k^{2-\alpha} \leqslant 2c C_2 b_n^{p - 2 + \eta(2-\alpha)} \to 0, \quad \text{for any }
p > 0.\qedhere
\]

body_md:
The necessity of $\beta_-\leqslant1\leqslant\beta_+$ for strongly eroded processes is established in~\cite[Prop.~1.6]{MR4828847}. It remains to show that the entire region can be attained. Fix $0\leqslant b_-\leqslant 1\leqslant b_+\leqslant 2$. 

\textbf{Part 1:} We start by constructing a smooth base process with indices $\beta_-=0$ and $\beta_+=b_+$. Define the sequences
\[
z_n = 2^{-(n!)^2},
\quad
a_n = \frac{nb_++3}{n+2}\in(1,2),
\quad
\ell_n = z_n^{-a_n},
\quad\text{and}\quad
h_n = \ell_n z_n^2 = z_n^{2-a_n}.
\]
Note that $a_n \to b_+\in[1,2]$ and $2-a_n \to 2-b_+\in[0,1]$ as $n \to \infty$.

Let $\varphi \in C^\infty(\mathbb{R})$ be an even, non-negative function supported in $[-1,1]$ with $\int_\mathbb{R} \varphi(u)\mathrm{d} u = 1$. Fix $\rho > 0$ and set $\kappa \coloneqq \int_\mathbb{R} (1+y/4)^2 \varphi(y)\mathrm{d} y$. Define the symmetric $C^\infty$ density on $\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0\}$ by
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:full-region-base-density}
\upsilon_+(x) = \rho e^{-x^2} + \sum_{n\geqslant1} \frac{4\ell_n}{z_n} \left( \varphi\left(\frac{4(x-z_n)}{z_n}\right) + \varphi\left(\frac{4(x+z_n)}{z_n}\right) \right) > 0.
\end{equation}
The background $\rho e^{-x^2}$ ensures $\upsilon_+$ is everywhere strictly positive, but only adds finite mass, so by~\cite[Prop.~1.5]{MR4828847} it affects neither strong erosion nor the indices $\beta_\pm$ nor the $C^\infty$ property of the transition laws. To simplify the estimates, we treat $\upsilon_+$ with $\rho=0$.

\textit{Valid L\'evy measure.} 
The bumps are centred at $\pm z_n$ and have radius $z_n/4$ (making their supports disjoint, as $5z_{n+1}/4< 3z_{n}/4$), total mass $2\ell_n$, and second moment $2\kappa h_n$. By definition of $a_n$, it follows that $2-a_n=(n(2-b_+)+1)/(n+2)$, implying that 
\begin{equation*}
(n+1)^2(2-a_{n+1})-(2-a_n) =
\frac{(n+1)^2}{n+3}-\frac{1}{n+2} +(2-b_+)\left(
\frac{(n+1)^3}{n+3}-\frac{n}{n+2}
\right) \geqslant
\frac{(n+1)^2}{n+3}-\frac{1}{n+2}
\geqslant 1,
\end{equation*} for all $n \geqslant 2$, and similarly, since $1<a_{n+1}<2$, we get that
\begin{equation*} 
(n+1)^2 a_{n+1} - a_n \geqslant (n+1)^2 - 2 \geqslant 2, \quad \text{for all }n \geqslant 1.
\end{equation*}
Next, since $z_{n+1} = z_n^{(n+1)^2}$, and $z_n \leqslant 1/4$, it follows that $h_{n+1}/h_n \leqslant z_n \leqslant 1/4$ and $\ell_{n-1}/\ell_n \leqslant z_{n-1}^2 \leqslant 1/16$ for $n \geqslant 2$. A geometric comparison thereby yields
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:full-region-geom-sums}
h_{n+1} \leqslant \sum_{k>n} h_k \leqslant 2h_{n+1},
\quad\text{and}\quad
\sum_{k<n} \ell_k \leqslant 2\ell_{n-1},
\quad\text{for all } n\geqslant 2.
\end{equation}
In particular, $\sum_{n\geqslant 1} h_n < \infty$, making $\upsilon_+$ a valid L\'evy density with finite second moment.

\textit{Strong erosion.}
Let $X$ have density $\upsilon_+$, zero Gaussian coefficient, and zero drift parameter. Set $r_n = 2z_n$ and $t_n = 2\kappa h_n$. The cutoff $(-r_n, r_n)$ contains precisely the bumps with $k \geqslant n$ and excludes all bumps with $k < n$. Symmetry gives $d(r_n) = 0$. We verify the three limits in~\eqref{gen:cutoff-conditions} as $n \to \infty$ sequentially:
\begin{gather*}
    \frac{r_n}{t_n} = \kappa^{-1} z_n^{a_n-1} \leqslant \kappa^{-1} 2^{-(n!)^2/(n+2)} \to 0, \quad 
0 \leqslant \frac{V(r_n)}{t_n} - 1 = \frac{\sum_{k>n}h_k}{h_n} \leqslant 2\frac{h_{n+1}}{h_n} \leqslant 2z_n \to 0,\\
t_n \overline{\nu}(r_n) \leqslant 8\kappa h_n \ell_{n-1} = 8\kappa z_{n-1}^{n^2(2-a_n) - a_{n-1}} \leqslant 8\kappa 2^{-\frac{n^2-2n-4}{n+2}((n-1)!)^2} \to 0.
\end{gather*}
Proposition~\ref{prop:gen-Gaussian} implies that $X$ is strongly eroded with $\mathfrak{s}_{1} \equiv \infty$. 

\textit{Activity indices.} Bounding $|x|^p$ on $[3z_n/4, 5z_n/4]$ shows that
\[
\kappa h_n\left(5z_n/4\right)^{p-2}
\leqslant \int_{3z_n/4}^{5z_n/4} x^p \upsilon_+(x)\mathrm{d} x
\leqslant \kappa h_n\left(3z_n/4\right)^{p-2}.
\]
Hence, summing over $n$, we obtain that
\[
\int_{(-1,1)} |x|^p \upsilon_+(x)\mathrm{d} x < \infty 
\quad \text{if and only if}\quad  \sum_{n\geqslant 1} h_n z_n^{p-2} = \sum_{n\geqslant 1} z_n^{p-a_n} < \infty.
\]
The series $\sum_{n\geqslant 1} z_n^{p-a_n}$ converges for $p > b_+$ and diverges for $p < b_+$, so $\beta_+(X) = b_+$. For the lower index, at $y_n = 3 z_n/4$ the cutoff excludes all bumps with $k \leqslant n$, giving
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:V_X-V}
y_n^{p-2} V(y_n) \leqslant 4\kappa y_n^{p-2} h_{n+1} = 4\kappa (3/4)^{p-2} z_n^{(n+1)^2(2-a_{n+1}) + p - 2} \to 0, \qquad \text{for any}\enskip p > 0.
\end{equation}
Thus, $\liminf_{y\downarrow0} y^{p-2}V(y) = 0$ for all $p > 0$, proving that $\beta_-(X) = 0$.

\textit{Smooth transition densities.} For $z_n^{-1} \leqslant |u| \leqslant z_{n+1}^{-1}$, the $n$-th bump pair yields $Q(u) \geqslant 2(1-q)\ell_n$ with $q \coloneqq \sup_{|u|\geqslant 1/4}|\widehat{\varphi}(u)| < 1$. Because $a_n > 1$, we have $\ell_n = z_n^{-a_n} \geqslant z_n^{-1}$. Since $\log(z_{n+1}^{-1}) = (n+1)^2(n!)^2\log 2$, it follows that
\[
\frac{Q(u)}{\log|u|} 
\geqslant \frac{2(1-q) 2^{(n!)^2}}{(n+1)^2(n!)^2\log 2}\to \infty,
\quad\text{as}\enskip |u| \to \infty.
\]
Thus, $\int_\mathbb{R} |u|^j e^{-tQ(u)}\mathrm{d} u < \infty$ for all $t > 0$ and $j \geqslant 0$, ensuring bounded $C^\infty$ transition densities with bounded derivatives of all orders.

\textbf{Part 2:} We will now alter the process to have the correct lower index. If $b_-=0$, the process $X$ satisfies all required properties. Assume instead $b_- \in (0,1]$. Let $\chi \in C^\infty(\mathbb{R})$ be even with $0 \leqslant \chi \leqslant 1$, $\chi = 1$ on $[-e^{-3},e^{-3}]$, and $\chi = 0$ outside $(-e^{-2},e^{-2})$. Define
\[
\upsilon_-(x) \coloneqq
\begin{cases}
\chi(x)|x|^{-1-b_-}, &b_- \in (0,1),\\
\chi(x)(|x|^2\log^2|x|)^{-1}, &b_-=1,
\end{cases}
\qquad\text{with}\quad \int_{\mathbb{R}}|x|\upsilon_-(x)\mathrm{d} x<\infty.
\]
The truncated variance $W(r) \coloneqq \int_{(-r,r)} x^2 \upsilon_-(x)\mathrm{d} x$ satisfies, for $r \in (0, e^{-3})$,
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:V_Y-W}
W(r) = \frac{2}{2-b_-} r^{2-b_-} \quad \text{for }b_-\in(0,1),
\quad\text{and}\quad
\frac{r}{\log^2(2/r)} \leqslant W(r) \leqslant \frac{2r}{\log^2(1/r)} \quad \text{for }b_- = 1.
\end{equation}
Consequently, as $r\downarrow 0$, $r^{p-2} W(r) \to \infty $ for every $p \in (0,b_-)$ and $r^{p-2} W(r) \to 0$ for every $p > b_-$.

Let $Y$ be an independent symmetric L\'evy process with density $\upsilon_-$, and set $Z = X + Y$, with density $\upsilon_+ + \upsilon_-$. Because $Y$ has finite variation, $Z$ is strongly eroded by~\cite[Prop.~1.5]{MR4828847}. Small-jump moments add, so $\beta_+(Z) = \max\{b_+, b_-\} = b_+$. For the lower index, $r^{p-2}V_Z(r) \geqslant r^{p-2}W(r) \to \infty$ for $p < b_-$, while along $y_n = 3z_n/4$, we have as $n \to \infty$,
\[
y_n^{p-2} V_Z(y_n) = y_n^{p-2} V(y_n) + y_n^{p-2} W(y_n) \to 0, \quad\text{for all } p > b_-,
\]
by~\eqref{eq:V_X-V} and~\eqref{eq:V_Y-W}. Thus $\beta_-(Z) = b_-$. Finally, the non-negative real exponent of $Y$ preserves the super-logarithmic Fourier growth and hence the smooth transition densities.
